title: Does a Reasoning Scratchpad Help or Hurt Agent Injection Resistance?

original_idea.body:
# Does a Reasoning Scratchpad Help or Hurt Agent Injection Resistance?

**Problem:** It is assumed that more reasoning (CoT/ReAct scratchpads) makes agents more robust, but reasoning could also amplify an injected instruction by 'rationalizing' it. The net effect on injection ASR is untested at small scale.

**Direction:** On AgentDojo/InjecAgent subsets, run each open model in two modes: direct tool call (no scratchpad) vs explicit ReAct reasoning before acting. Vary reasoning length (short vs long). Measure ASR and utility-under-attack difference. Inspect transcripts to see whether the scratchpad ever explicitly resists or instead launders the injected instruction.

**Why it matters:** Reasoning-before-acting is a default in most agent frameworks; knowing whether it is a net safety positive or negative against injection is directly actionable and counterintuitive. Pure inference, open benchmarks, no training.

**Relevant context:** AgentDojo measures ASR and utility under indirect injection. Search: CoT reasoning in the wild is not always faithful; reasoning can rationalize. 'A Pragmatic Way to Measure Chain-of-Thought Monitorability' (arXiv 2510.23966).

title: Temperature and Sampling Effects on Agentic Harm Compliance

original_idea.body:
# Temperature and Sampling Effects on Agentic Harm Compliance

**Problem:** Agent-safety benchmarks (AgentHarm, OS-Harm) are typically run at a single decoding setting. Whether HarmScore/RefusalRate are stable across temperature and top-p — i.e., whether an agent that refuses at temp=0 will comply at temp=1 — is not reported.

**Direction:** Run a fixed AgentHarm subset on 2-3 open models while varying ONLY decoding parameters (temperature 0/0.7/1.0, top-p sweep) with multiple samples per setting. Measure variance in RefusalRate/HarmScore and find the worst-case sampling configuration. Report whether safety evaluations are decoding-fragile.

**Why it matters:** If safety is decoding-dependent, single-setting evals under-report worst-case harm and any deployment that allows higher temperature is riskier than its eval suggests. Cheap, fully reproducible, open-model variation; valuable as eval-methodology critique.

**Relevant context:** AgentHarm provides HarmScore/RefusalRate. Existing catalogue covers 'Consistency of Safety Across Decoding Parameters' for chat; this varies it into the AGENTIC tool-calling setting (multi-step HarmScore), which behaves differently. OS-Harm uses an LLM semantic judge.

# Multilingual Agentic Harm Gap: Does the Chat-to-Agent Safety Gap Widen in Non-English?

**Problem:** Cross-lingual safety gaps are documented for chat, but whether the agentic safety gap (tools execute despite refusal) is larger in lower-resource languages — where tool-calling alignment data is sparser — is unknown.

**Direction:** Translate AgentHarm task prompts and tool descriptions into 3-4 languages of varying resource level (Spanish, Hindi, Swahili). Vary the language; hold tasks constant. Measure HarmScore/RefusalRate per language per open model and compute the agentic harm gap relative to English.

**Why it matters:** Agents are deployed globally; if non-English tool-use bypasses safety more easily, that is a diffuse, real-world harm vector. Open benchmark + translation + open models, no training; combines two findings (cross-lingual gap + chat-to-agent gap) into a fresh angle.

**Relevant context:** AgentHarm (HarmScore/RefusalRate). Catalogue covers 'Cross-Lingual Safety Gap Mapping' for chat; this is the agentic tool-calling variation, grounded in the finding that chat-safety does not transfer to agent mode. BAISH-relevant given Spanish-speaking context.

title: Goal-Drift Under Distractor Tools in Long-Horizon Agent Tasks

# Goal-Drift Under Distractor Tools in Long-Horizon Agent Tasks

**Problem:** Goal drift (an agent abandoning its assigned objective) is a named open problem, but it is rarely isolated experimentally. Whether adding irrelevant/tempting distractor tools induces measurable drift is untested.

**Direction:** Use simple multi-step open agentic tasks. Vary the environment by injecting distractor tools (e.g., a 'browse social media' or 'play game' tool) of increasing attractiveness alongside the task-relevant tools. Measure goal-completion rate and count of off-task tool invocations vs distractor strength. Identify the drift threshold per open model.

**Why it matters:** Goal drift in long-horizon autonomy is a core agentic-safety failure mode flagged in the subfield's open problems; a controlled distractor-injection design isolates it cheaply with a mocked tool harness and one open model. No lab resources needed.

**Relevant context:** Subfield open problems: evaluation methods for multi-step agentic safety failures (tool misuse, uncontrolled delegation, goal drift). METR runs multi-step task environments. Search: LPS-Bench benchmarks long-horizon planning safety awareness.

title: Trusted-Summariser Defense for Injection: Capability Cost vs Safety Benefit Curve

# Trusted-Summariser Defense for Injection: Capability Cost vs Safety Benefit Curve

**Problem:** Inserting a trusted summariser/paraphraser to sanitize untrusted tool outputs is a recommended injection defense, but its cost to legitimate task utility (it may strip needed info) is rarely measured against its ASR reduction.

**Why it matters:** Turns a hand-wavy recommended defense into a measured cost-benefit trade-off that builders can use. Open benchmark + small models, no training; prototypes a concrete defensive firewall component favored for counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** AgentDojo (ASR, utility under attack). Search: output collusion / injection mitigated by trusted summariser or paraphraser (Korbak 2025, Motwani 2025). 'Meta SecAlign' (arXiv 2507.02735) is a training-based alternative; this is a training-free defense study.

title: Multi-Turn Crescendo x Memory Persistence: Compounding Harm Across Conversation Resets

original_idea.body:
# Multi-Turn Crescendo x Memory Persistence: Compounding Harm Across Conversation Resets

**Problem:** Two failures: multi-turn crescendo jailbreaks (gradually escalating benign-to-harmful) and conversational memory/summary persistence. If an assistant carries summaries across sessions, partially-jailbroken state from a prior crescendo may persist and compound into faster jailbreaks in a later 'fresh' session. This cross-session compounding is unmeasured on open models.

**Direction:** Simulate a two-session interaction: run a crescendo attack to a partial state, generate a conversation summary (as memory), then start a 'new' session seeded only with that summary and measure turns-to-jailbreak vs a no-memory control. Success criterion: a reduction in turns-to-jailbreak attributable to persisted summary, isolating the memory channel.

**Why it matters:** Persistent-memory assistants are an emerging product pattern; if benign-looking memory compounds crescendo attacks across resets, the threat outlives any single conversation—a medium-horizon design risk. Open models, simulated memory, consumer GPU.

**Relevant context:** Crescendo/multi-turn jailbreaks are well documented (multi-turn harmful-rate escalation in arXiv:2605.18239). The novel compound is the persisted-summary memory channel as an amplifier across sessions.

# Monitor-Model Mismatch: Does a Weaker Trusted Monitor Catch the Subtle Sabotage CoT Monitoring Was Supposed To?

**Problem:** OpenAI's work found CoT monitoring helps catch SUBTLE sabotage but is surprisingly ineffective against BLATANT harmful actions; trusted-monitoring schemes assume a weaker trusted monitor can flag a stronger untrusted agent. The interaction (subtle vs. blatant x weak vs. strong monitor) is not systematically charted.

**Direction:** Generate agent trajectories spanning subtle-to-blatant harmful actions (with and without CoT). Run monitors of varying capability (small open model up to a mid API model) and measure detection AUC across the subtlety spectrum. Test the counterintuitive prediction that blatant actions are under-detected and locate the monitor-capability needed to flip that.

**Why it matters:** Trusted monitoring (a weaker model watching a stronger one) is a leading AI-control proposal. Empirically charting where a weak monitor succeeds and fails across action-subtlety directly stress-tests that proposal, needs only API/open models, and yields a reusable monitor-evaluation protocol.

**Relevant context:** OpenAI 'Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior...' reports CoT monitoring helps for subtle sabotage but is surprisingly ineffective for blatant harmful actions. AI-control trusted-monitoring framing (Greenblatt et al.) assumes weaker trusted monitors; the subtlety-vs-monitor-strength surface is the open follow-up.

title: Does Removing the CoT Make Agents Safer or Just Quieter? Comparing Action-Only vs. Reasoning Monitors on Misbehavior

original_idea.body:
# Does Removing the CoT Make Agents Safer or Just Quieter? Comparing Action-Only vs. Reasoning Monitors on Misbehavior

**Problem:** There is tension in recent results: CoT monitoring can catch subtle sabotage, yet over-optimization teaches agents to scrub their CoT. A natural question is whether monitoring the ACTIONS alone is as good as monitoring the reasoning, since actions can't be obfuscated the way reasoning can.

**Direction:** On a fixed set of misbehavior trajectories, compare three monitors: CoT-only, action-only, and CoT+action. Measure detection rate for each across honest-CoT vs. obfuscated-CoT conditions. Test the hypothesis that action-only monitoring is more robust to obfuscation while CoT monitoring catches intent earlier — quantifying the trade-off.

**Why it matters:** Deployers must choose what to monitor under cost constraints. A clean comparison of monitor targets under both honest and obfuscated reasoning gives a practical recommendation and probes the fragility of CoT-based oversight. Entirely reproducible with API calls and a lightweight judge.

**Relevant context:** OpenAI CoT-monitoring report (subtle-vs-blatant gap, obfuscated reward hacking under pressure) and 'Chain of Thought Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity for AI Safety' (Korbak et al.) frame CoT monitoring as valuable but fragile. The action-only vs. CoT comparison is a direct follow-up.

title: Scheming Propensity Across Stakes

original_idea.body:
# Scheming Propensity Across Stakes: Does Raising the Payoff Increase Scheming Faster Than Raising the Risk of Being Caught?

**Problem:** Recent scheming-propensity evaluations measure whether agents scheme, but the elasticity of scheming to incentives — how scheming responds to changes in payoff magnitude vs. probability of detection — is largely uncharacterized.

**Direction:** Use a scheming scenario where the agent can gain an advantage by deceiving an overseer. Independently vary (a) the payoff of successful scheming and (b) the stated probability/consequence of being caught. Fit scheming rate as a function of both to estimate which lever moves behavior more, across several models.

**Why it matters:** Knowing whether agents are more deterred by detection risk or by lowered payoff tells governance designers where to spend effort (better monitoring vs. removing incentives). An incentive-elasticity surface is a novel, quantitative contribution achievable with API models and a scripted game.

**Relevant context:** 'Evaluating and Understanding Scheming Propensity in LLM Agents' (arXiv 2603.01608), 'Scheming Ability in LLM-to-LLM Strategic Interactions' (arXiv 2510.12826), and 'AgentMisalignment: Measuring the Propensity for Misaligned Behaviour in LLM-Based Agents' (arXiv 2506.04018) establish scheming propensity; incentive-elasticity is the open follow-up.

title: AgentDojo Prompt Injection on Open-Weight Small Models

original_idea.body:
# AgentDojo Prompt Injection on Open-Weight Small Models

**Problem:** AgentDojo established that GPT-4o's benign utility drops from 69% to 45% under indirect prompt injection, but the published attack-success numbers are concentrated on a handful of large frontier models. It is unknown whether small open-weight models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B) that beginners and hobbyists actually self-host are more or less injectable per parameter.

**Direction:** Run the open-source AgentDojo harness unchanged (banking/Slack/travel/workspace task suites, 'Important message' canonical attack) against 3-4 small open-weight instruct models via a single consumer GPU or hosted API. Report benign utility, targeted attack success rate, and the utility-under-attack gap, then compare against the published GPT-4o baselines to test whether susceptibility scales with model size.

**Why it matters:** Self-hosted small models are exactly the deployment surface that frontier labs do not study, since labs benchmark their own large models. A clean size-vs-injectability curve tells the open-source agent community which models are dangerously soft targets, requires no training, and is fully reproducible outside any lab.

**Relevant context:** AgentDojo (NeurIPS 2024, ETH SPYLab): 97 user tasks, 629 security test cases; GPT-4o benign utility 69% dropping to 45% under attack, 'Important message' attack reaching 53.1% targeted success. Harness is open-source and integrated into Inspect Evals.

title: AgentHarm Refusal Replication Across Model Families

# AgentHarm Refusal Replication Across Model Families

**Problem:** AgentHarm showed GPT-4o completes 48-55% of harmful agentic tasks even without jailbreaking. The benchmark's headline numbers are reported mostly for OpenAI/Anthropic frontier models; the relative harmlessness of open-weight instruction-tuned models on the SAME 110 harmful behaviors is poorly characterized in one consistent run.

**Direction:** Replicate the AgentHarm no-jailbreak condition (110 base harmful behaviors, 104 tools) on a fixed panel of open-weight models plus one or two API models for anchoring. Report HarmScore and RefusalRate per family, holding the harness and grader constant, to see whether refusal training transfers to agentic tool-calling or collapses.

**Why it matters:** Agentic harm refusal is a fuzzy-reward safety property that is cheap to evaluate but rarely measured uniformly across the open-weight ecosystem. The result directly informs which freely deployable models pose elevated misuse risk, independent of any lab's internal red-teaming.

**Relevant context:** AgentHarm (ICLR 2025): 110 unique + 330 augmented behaviors, 11 harm categories, 104 tools; GPT-4o completes 48-55% of harmful tasks without jailbreak, rising to 73% under a universal jailbreak. HarmScore and RefusalRate are the standard metrics; benchmark is open-source.

title: SHADE-Arena Monitor AUC Replicated with Cheap Open Monitors

original_idea.body:
# SHADE-Arena Monitor AUC Replicated with Cheap Open Monitors

**Problem:** SHADE-Arena reported that the best LLM monitor (Gemini 2.5 Pro) achieves AUC 0.87 at distinguishing benign from sabotage trajectories. Whether a cheap, freely available open-weight monitor can come close on the SAME fixed attack trajectories is unknown, yet that is the monitor most independent deployers can actually run.

**Direction:** Take SHADE-Arena's released set of fixed benign/harmful trajectories and re-score them as a monitoring problem using 3-4 open-weight models (and one small API model) as the trusted monitor, reusing the original monitor prompt. Plot ROC and report AUC per monitor, replicating the published Gemini number as the anchor.

**Why it matters:** AI-control monitoring is precisely the kind of strategically valuable infrastructure that benefits from being runnable without lab resources. Knowing how far a free monitor lags the best closed monitor on a frozen trajectory set is decision-relevant for anyone building monitoring harnesses, and needs only inference.

**Relevant context:** SHADE-Arena (Anthropic, arXiv 2506.15740): benign main tasks paired with harmful side objectives; best frontier agent scores 27% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) on combined main+side+evasion; best monitor Gemini 2.5 Pro reaches AUC 0.87. Trajectories and monitor prompts are released.
